title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA engineers show that sparse attention shifts long-context cost into the indexer and Top-k (47% of DeepSeek V3.2 prefill at 128K), and use FP8 kernel sweeps to issue eight GPU co-design guidelines: KH=1 with cross-head reduction, G x (D+1) within one ~200-row Tensor Core tile, FP16 epilogue, Hsz 128, fewer scored keys, fused/guess-based Top-k (2.1-2.4x), and large-block selection.

insights.claim: Agentic workloads, long documents and large codebases are pushing LLM context lengths from tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens, and at 128K tokens dense attention can consume most of a transformer layer's prefill time.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Long-context agentic demand makes attention efficiency, not just FLOPs, the binding inference cost driver for GPU fleets.
insights.quote: at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer
insights.locator: Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases

insights.claim: Sparse attention does not eliminate the long-context cost; it moves it into the indexer, which still scores all N keys of the context to choose the k (typically a few thousand) keys each query attends to.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: The indexer and Top-k kernels become the new optimization frontier and a place where hardware vendors' kernel stacks differentiate.
insights.quote: The cost does not disappear; it moves into the indexer.
insights.locator: What is sparse attention and why does it matter?

insights.claim: In DeepSeek V3.2's sparse attention (DSA), the indexer and Top-k selection together take 47% of the per-layer prefill time at a 128K-token input, versus dense MLA in DeepSeek-R1.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Nearly half of sparse-attention prefill time sits in selection overhead, so fused indexer/Top-k kernels are a meaningful throughput lever.
insights.quote: the indexer and Top-k take 47% of the DeepSeek V3.2 prefill layer

insights.claim: Frontier sparse-attention designs have largely converged on one indexer key head, 32-64 query heads reduced by ReLU plus weighted sum, a 128 head dimension, and token or small-block selection, as seen in DeepSeek DSA, GLM 5.2, GLM 5.3 Flash, LongCat LSA-Flash, CSA and Qwen QSA; MiniMax MSA, NSA and MoBA diverge.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Sparse attention is now mainstream across Chinese frontier labs (DeepSeek, Zhipu GLM, Qwen, MiniMax, LongCat), and NVIDIA is steering their design choices toward its GPU strengths.

insights.claim: The sparse-attention indexer is one batched matmul with a fused epilogue: compute-bound in prefill but memory-bound in decode, where it streams the whole key cache from HBM to produce only a few rows of logits.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Decode-phase sparse attention remains HBM-bandwidth bound, reinforcing the value of memory bandwidth in inference GPUs.

insights.claim: Indexer arithmetic intensity is proportional to the group size G = query heads / key heads, while sequence length and compression ratio scale total work but not the FLOPs-to-bytes ratio; designs without cross-head reduction such as MiniMax MSA and MoBA lose that factor.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Model architectures that reduce heads to one logit per key extract more value per byte moved on GPUs.
insights.quote: Designs without this reduction (MSA, MoBA) lose that factor.
insights.locator: Three observations follow from Equations 1 and 2

insights.claim: On NVIDIA GPUs, growing indexer group size 16x moves decode runtime only 2% because the single key-cache read sets runtime, while in prefill doubling G from 8 to 16 costs 1.66x rather than 2x due to the FP32 logit write.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Extra query heads are nearly free in decode, so models can add indexer heads without hurting serving latency.
insights.quote: Decode runtime moves only 2% while 𝐺 grows 16x
insights.locator: Query heads, group size, and speculative draft length

insights.claim: Speculative-decoding draft tokens are nearly free for the sparse-attention indexer as long as G x (D+1) fits in one Tensor Core tile of about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue): runtime rises only 1.37x and 1.87x while work grows 6x and 26x at G=32 and G=8.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Speculative decoding and sparse attention are complementary on NVIDIA hardware, within a hard tile-size budget model designers must respect.
insights.quote: the draft tokens are nearly free while they fit in one pass

insights.claim: Running the indexer epilogue in FP16 widens the tile to 256 rows and yields 1.31x decode speedup at G=64, D+1=4, and FP16 matmul accumulation reaches 1.45x if QK scaling keeps outputs within FP16 range.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Lower-precision paths keep delivering inference throughput gains, favoring hardware with strong low-precision support.

insights.claim: Increasing indexer key heads from 1 to 8 grows decode runtime linearly, 7.6x, because each key head requires another full key-cache read, while prefill grows only 1.3x to 1.6x.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Multi-key-head indexer designs carry a large decode serving-cost penalty; NVIDIA recommends KH = 1 with cross-head reduction.
insights.quote: runtime grows linearly with KH: 7.6x from KH = 1 to 8

insights.claim: An indexer head dimension of 64 leaves Tensor Cores waiting on the CUDA-core epilogue in prefill (64 to 128 costs only 1.1x-1.2x), while decode pays for every extra key byte, so most designs settle at Hsz = 128.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Explains industry convergence on 128-dim indexer heads as a hardware-driven, not accuracy-driven, choice.
insights.quote: Hsz = 64 leaves the Tensor Cores waiting on the epilogue.

insights.claim: Scoring fewer keys, via compressed indexer keys, hierarchical indexing, or index sharing across layers, is the only way to reduce indexer work; runtime scales linearly with 1/compression ratio in both prefill and decode.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Compression and index sharing are the main remaining levers for cutting long-context inference cost per token.
insights.quote: Scoring fewer keys is the only way to reduce indexer work.

insights.claim: Top-k selection cost follows the number of keys scored rather than k: each doubling of key count costs about 1.7x in prefill and 1.5x in decode, while 64x larger k raises Top-k time under 2x.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Model designers can afford larger k budgets; the cost driver is context length scored.
insights.quote: Its cost follows the keys scored, not 𝑘.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k in TensorRT LLM reuses the previous decode step's selection as a guess and is 2.1x to 2.4x faster than standard radix select on DeepSeek V3.2 and DeepSeek V4 decode.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's software stack is being tuned specifically for DeepSeek's latest models, deepening the CUDA/TensorRT moat for Chinese open-weight model serving.
insights.quote: it is 2.1x to 2.4x faster than a standard radix select
insights.locator: Two kernel techniques reduce Top-k cost further

insights.claim: Fusing Top-k into the indexer kernel eliminates the logit write and read-back, saving time, HBM capacity and data-movement energy; FlashInfer's selective Top-k path is an open-source example that never writes the full logits matrix.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Kernel fusion in open-source serving stacks (FlashInfer) lowers memory and energy per token for sparse models.
insights.locator: Second, fusing Top-k into the indexer

insights.claim: Block-level sparse selection (GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MSA, MoBA) lets core attention fetch keys and values in bulk and share fetches across queries, whereas token-level selection (DSA, GLM 5.2, LSA) scatters fetches that queries rarely share.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Architecture choice between token and block sparsity materially affects serving efficiency on GPUs; NVIDIA favors large blocks.

insights.claim: At a fixed budget of 2,048 selected keys per query, core attention runtime follows the number of blocks processed, so halving the block size nearly doubles runtime in both prefill and decode.
insights.speaker: Timmy Liu
insights.so_what: Large selection blocks (and large core-attention group sizes so many query heads share each KV head) are the hardware-friendly design path.
insights.quote: Halving the block size nearly doubles runtime in both prefill and decode.
